case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Heck v. Humphrey favorable-termination bar prevents a §1983 plaintiff—who has an outstanding criminal conviction arising from the same incident—from pursuing prospective declaratory or injunctive relief challenging the constitutionality of a municipal policy or ordinance.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (as limited by the judge-made doctrine of Heck v. Humphrey) and the U.S. Constitution’s First Amendment (as the substantive basis for the requested prospective relief against the City’s enforcement practices/ordinance).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Olivier argues that Heck’s bar is aimed at damages actions that would functionally undermine an outstanding conviction and should not block forward-looking relief (injunction/declaration) that targets ongoing or future enforcement of allegedly unconstitutional municipal rules; he contends that allowing Heck to foreclose prospective relief improperly insulates unconstitutional speech restrictions from review, chills protected expression, and prevents plaintiffs from obtaining meaningful relief where the real injury is the continuing threat of enforcement rather than retrospective compensation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The City argues that Heck should apply to Olivier’s suit because the requested relief would necessarily imply the invalidity of his still-outstanding conviction (or would operate as an end-run around habeas-like limits), and in any event the case is a poor vehicle due to independent procedural and merits defects—e.g., forfeiture/presentment problems noted in the Fifth Circuit, and potential preclusion/estoppel/res judicata issues—such that even a petitioner win on the Heck question would only lead to remand and likely dismissal on other grounds.
key_precedents: Siders v. City of Brandon, Mississippi

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest institutional point: an as-applied declaratory or injunctive judgment can function as a collateral attack if, in this record, the only path to relief is a determination that the ordinance was unconstitutional as applied to the very conduct of conviction, and Edwards v. Balisok confirms labels do not control. But that argument goes to how the “necessarily imply” test applies here, not to adopting a categorical bar on forward-looking First Amendment challenges; Wilkinson v. Dotson’s “ordinarily” language supports a remedy-specific, case-by-case inquiry rather than a per se rule. The minimal and legitimacy-preserving course is to hold that §1983 is not categorically unavailable for prospective relief, while making clear that on remand the decree must be dismissed or narrowed if granting it would, by its own terms and logical effect, negate an element essential to the outstanding conviction. Justice Thomas’s point that this record may fall on the Heck side can be accommodated through that remand-tailoring approach without expanding a judge-made limitation beyond its rationale.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan argue that an injunction can be tailored to regulate only future enforcement and thus avoid necessarily implying invalidity under Wilkinson, but that framing does not fit this record: the plaintiff’s requested declaration/injunction is premised on the ordinance being unconstitutional as applied to the very conduct of conviction. Edwards v. Balisok confirms, as Justice Alito stresses, that remedial labels do not control; we look to the logical effect of success, and here success would negate an essential predicate for a still-outstanding judgment. Wilkinson’s “ordinarily” language does not create a safe harbor where prospective relief can be granted only by adjudicating the unconstitutionality of the conviction’s predicate law, functioning as a collateral attack. Although I agree Heck is a judge-made limitation and should be kept narrow given §1983’s text, even on that narrow view this suit falls within Heck’s necessary-implication bar.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed case-by-case tailoring under Wilkinson v. Dotson has surface appeal, but it elides Heck’s practical-consequences inquiry: if the only way to enjoin future enforcement “as applied” is to adjudicate that the ordinance was unconstitutional as applied to the very conduct of conviction, success necessarily implies the conviction lacked a lawful predicate. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett argue a decree can disclaim any adjudication of the conviction’s validity, but Edwards v. Balisok teaches that remedial labels and disclaimers cannot defeat the logical-effect test when the judgment’s operative premise negates what sustained the punishment. Justice Kavanaugh is right that this record is not a separable procedural challenge; it is a substantive attack on the rule that supplied an essential element, and allowing it under §1983 invites an end-run around finality and habeas-channeling. Wilkinson’s “ordinarily” language supports, rather than undermines, treating this as the atypical case where prospective framing cannot avoid necessary implication.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh press the hardest point: that an as-applied declaration/injunction can be an end-run around habeas because it would, in substance, condemn the predicate for an outstanding conviction, and Edwards v. Balisok shows Heck is not defeated by remedial labels. But Wilkinson v. Dotson still requires a remedy-specific inquiry into whether the judgment, by its own operative terms, would necessarily invalidate the conviction or shorten custody; a forward-looking injunction can be tailored (as the Chief and Justice Kagan propose) to regulate future enforcement and expressly disclaim any adjudication of the conviction’s validity. Balisok is different because the relief necessarily impeached the validity of the deprivation decision itself, whereas here the asserted injury is ongoing chill and threat of future enforcement that warrants prospective §1983 review absent a decree that negates an element essential to the conviction. Finality concerns can be handled on remand through narrowing the requested relief and ordinary preclusion/justiciability doctrines, rather than expanding a judge-made Heck bar to insulate ongoing First Amendment violations from any prospective remedy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Alito press the hardest point: an as-applied declaration/injunction can be an end-run around habeas, and Edwards v. Balisok teaches that labels don’t defeat Heck. But Heck’s operative limit is logical necessity—whether the judgment in this §1983 case would itself “necessarily imply” invalidity—and Wilkinson v. Dotson’s treatment of forward-looking relief (even with its “ordinarily” qualifier) supports allowing claims where the decree can be framed to regulate future enforcement and expressly avoid adjudicating the conviction’s validity. I agree with Justice Thomas that some declaratory relief necessarily undermines the punishment decision (as in Balisok), yet that logic doesn’t automatically carry over where the court can tailor relief to prospective application without negating any element of the existing judgment. Pragmatically, the administrable middle ground Chief Justice Roberts describes—reject a categorical bar, remand for tailoring/dismissal if the specific relief sought necessarily implies invalidity—answers the end-run concern without expanding a judge-made Heck limitation beyond its text-anchored rationale.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Alito make the strongest point that an “as-applied” declaration can be an end-run around habeas when success would necessarily negate a lawful predicate of the conviction, and Edwards v. Balisok confirms we look past remedial labels to logical effect. But that is precisely why I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that the Fifth Circuit’s categorical bar is overbroad: Wilkinson v. Dotson and Preiser require a claim-and-remedy-specific inquiry into whether the judgment, by its own force, would invalidate the conviction or shorten custody, not whether it would merely be rhetorically inconsistent or useful in later collateral proceedings. On this record, courts can police the end-run concern by narrowing or denying any relief that necessarily declares the past application unconstitutional in a way that negates an element essential to the outstanding judgment, while still permitting genuinely prospective relief regulating future enforcement. Extending Heck to foreclose all forward-looking First Amendment challenges would add a nontextual, judge-made limitation to §1983 and risks insulating ongoing constitutional violations from any judicial forum.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett make the strongest case that Wilkinson v. Dotson preserves §1983 for “ordinarily” prospective relief and that courts can tailor decrees to regulate only future enforcement, but that framing does not fit this record: the relief sought is expressly “as applied” to Olivier’s conduct of conviction and thus requires a determination that the ordinance was unconstitutional in the very application that supplied an element/predicate for the still-valid judgment. Edwards v. Balisok matters here because it confirms that declaratory/injunctive labels do not control when success would, in practical effect, undermine the validity of the outstanding judgment; the necessary-implication test still bars the suit when the only route to prospective relief is to brand the conviction’s legal basis unlawful. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrowing is institutionally attractive in the abstract, but as Justice Alito emphasizes, a case-by-case ‘tailoring’ approach becomes unworkable if it permits plaintiffs to plead around Heck by recasting a collateral attack as forward-looking—finality and habeas-channeling are better protected by requiring favorable termination first on these facts. I would leave open, consistent with Wilkinson, that genuinely separable challenges to future enforcement untethered to the conviction’s factual predicate may proceed, but this one cannot.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest objection: that an as-applied declaratory or injunctive judgment can be an end-run around habeas by functionally condemning the predicate for an outstanding conviction, and Edwards v. Balisok confirms labels do not control. But Heck’s limiting principle—whether success “necessarily implies” invalidity—remains the textual-anchor, and Wilkinson v. Dotson’s distinction is dispositive: prospective relief that regulates future enforcement does not, by its own operative terms, vacate the conviction or shorten custody, even if it supplies persuasive ammunition in later collateral proceedings. Justice Thomas is right that this record may be unusually intertwined with the conduct of conviction, but that counsels tailoring and careful framing on remand (or dismissal if the only coherent decree would negate an essential element), not a categorical expansion of a judge-made favorable-termination rule beyond its rationale. Under an originalist/textualist approach attentive to the enacted breadth of §1983 and the Court’s own “necessarily imply” line, the proper course is a case-specific logical-effect inquiry rather than a blanket bar on forward-looking First Amendment challenges.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that, under Edwards v. Balisok, declaratory or injunctive labels do not avoid Heck when the operative effect of success is to negate the lawful predicate of an outstanding conviction. But that only re-states the “necessarily implies” inquiry, and I agree with the Chief and Justice Kagan that Wilkinson v. Dotson cautions against converting that standard into a categorical bar on forward-looking §1983 relief, especially where a decree can be tailored to regulate future enforcement and expressly avoid adjudicating the conviction’s validity. On this record, the proper course is to reject the Fifth Circuit’s across-the-board rule and remand to assess whether the particular relief sought, as framed or as narrowed, would itself logically require a determination that invalidates an essential element of the conviction; if so, Heck applies, and if not, §1983 remains available. Under my pragmatic, procedure-focused approach, expanding Heck here would risk insulating ongoing First Amendment chilling effects from any prospective judicial check, when conventional tailoring and justiciability doctrines can address the end-run concern case-specifically.

John Roberts.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars §1983 claims only when success would "necessarily imply" the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, a limitation tied to preventing end-runs around habeas and preserving finality. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson, forward-looking declaratory or injunctive relief may proceed under §1983 when it targets future enforcement and does not itself require setting aside the prior conviction; an injunction against a municipal policy typically does not operate retroactively to invalidate past judgments. A narrow ruling recognizing that distinction best respects precedent and institutional legitimacy while preserving a path to prospective First Amendment review of ongoing municipal enforcement. Any vehicle or forfeiture issues can be addressed on remand without expanding Heck beyond its "necessarily imply" rationale.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1983 contains no textual “favorable-termination” requirement; Heck v. Humphrey is a judge-made limitation grounded in common-law analogies and concerns about collateral attacks on criminal judgments, so I would apply it only insofar as a §1983 claim would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding conviction. Here, Olivier’s requested declaration or injunction against enforcement of the ordinance—if it rests on the premise that the ordinance is unconstitutional as applied to the very conduct for which he stands convicted—would function as an impermissible end-run around the habeas/§1983 boundary recognized in Preiser v. Rodriguez and reaffirmed in Wilkinson v. Dotson. Because success would necessarily call the existing conviction into question, Heck’s favorable-termination bar applies, and Olivier must first obtain relief from the conviction through the appropriate channels before pursuing this §1983 action for prospective relief. The Constitution’s structure of limited federal judicial power and respect for final criminal judgments counsels against using §1983 to undermine a state conviction indirectly.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars a §1983 action when success would “necessarily imply” the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, and that principle should not turn on the plaintiff’s remedial label if the practical effect is the same. Where a plaintiff seeks a declaration or injunction that the municipal policy he was convicted under is unconstitutional as applied to his conduct, that relief would function as an end-run around habeas-like limits and would undermine the finality of the still-valid conviction, contrary to Heck’s common-law favorable-termination rule. Edwards v. Balisok confirms that Heck’s logic extends beyond damages at least to declaratory relief when the claim’s success would necessarily imply invalidity, and the Court should apply that same necessary-implication inquiry to prospective relief here. Given the law-enforcement and finality interests at stake, and the Fifth Circuit’s vehicle concerns, I would affirm and hold the action barred to the extent it necessarily implies the conviction’s invalidity.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey is a judge-made limitation designed to prevent §1983 damages actions from operating as a collateral attack on an outstanding conviction, and it is properly understood at the §1983/habeas boundary identified in Preiser v. Rodriguez. Where a plaintiff seeks only prospective declaratory or injunctive relief against ongoing enforcement of an allegedly unconstitutional municipal policy, the suit does not necessarily imply the invalidity of the past conviction in the way Heck targets, and this Court has recognized that “an otherwise proper injunction enjoining the prospective enforcement of invalid … regulations” may proceed under §1983. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms that the Heck line focuses on channeling challenges that would invalidate the fact or duration of custody into habeas, not broadly insulating ongoing unconstitutional rules from review. Given the practical impact on First Amendment rights and the need for meaningful forward-looking relief—especially for those facing continuing threat of enforcement—I would not extend Heck to categorically bar this prospective §1983 action.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey limits §1983 when success would functionally operate as a collateral attack on an outstanding conviction—i.e., when the claim would “necessarily imply” its invalidity—reflecting the division between §1983 and habeas. But this Court has distinguished forward-looking relief from that habeas core, explaining that “an otherwise proper injunction enjoining the prospective enforcement of invalid … regulations” is not barred, and that “ordinarily” prospective injunctive relief will not necessarily imply invalidity. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms that the Heck line is aimed at channeling challenges that would invalidate the fact or duration of confinement into habeas, not insulating ongoing enforcement policies from constitutional review under §1983. So unless the particular declaratory/injunctive relief sought would by its terms negate an element necessary to sustain Olivier’s conviction, Heck should not categorically bar the prospective First Amendment challenge to the City’s ordinance or enforcement policy.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1983’s text authorizes suits in equity as well as damages, and Heck v. Humphrey’s judge-made favorable-termination bar should not be extended beyond its rationale to foreclose forward-looking relief that does not seek to set aside a conviction. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson, the proper question is whether the §1983 claim would “necessarily imply” the invalidity of the outstanding conviction; a request to enjoin or declare unconstitutional a municipal policy’s future enforcement can proceed where success would not itself negate the conviction’s validity. Preiser v. Rodriguez channels into habeas only those claims whose core objective is immediate or speedier release, and prospective First Amendment relief against ongoing enforcement practices is not such a claim. Expanding Heck to categorically bar prospective challenges would unduly insulate potentially unconstitutional ordinances from review and improperly enlarges a nontextual limitation on §1983.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Heck v. Humphrey, a §1983 action is barred when a judgment for the plaintiff would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction, and that inquiry turns on the effect of the judgment rather than the label of the remedy. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms the same rule applies across forms of relief: if success would necessarily undermine the conviction or its lawful basis, §1983 cannot be used as a functional end-run around habeas limits recognized in Preiser v. Rodriguez. Here, petitioner seeks declaratory and injunctive relief that attacks the constitutionality of the very ordinance/policy under which he was convicted, which would directly call that conviction’s validity into question, triggering Heck’s favorable-termination requirement. Given the Court’s institutional interest in workable lines and respect for final criminal judgments, the Fifth Circuit’s application of Heck in these circumstances should be affirmed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey is a judge-made limitation on §1983 designed to prevent plaintiffs from using §1983 to mount a de facto collateral attack on an outstanding conviction—i.e., where success would "necessarily imply" the conviction’s invalidity. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson and the Preiser line, the dividing line is whether the relief sought lies in the "core of habeas"; forward-looking declaratory or injunctive relief that regulates future enforcement of an allegedly unconstitutional ordinance ordinarily does not invalidate (or necessarily imply the invalidity of) a past conviction. Wolff v. McDonnell and Edwards v. Balisok confirm that prospective injunctive relief is generally outside Heck’s bar even when a related conviction exists. To the extent the City raises vehicle or procedural defects, those are distinct from the threshold Heck scope question and do not justify expanding Heck beyond its rationale.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars §1983 suits only when success would "necessarily imply" the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, a limit this Court reaffirmed when it allowed prospective declaratory and injunctive challenges that do not automatically invalidate a conviction or shorten custody. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson, forward-looking relief aimed at changing future enforcement practices or procedures remains cognizable under §1983 so long as it does not function as a de facto collateral attack on the conviction itself; the Fifth Circuit’s broader approach risks insulating ongoing First Amendment violations from review and chilling protected speech. Procedural fairness and practical consequences counsel against extending a judge-made bar to foreclose all prospective relief where the plaintiff’s injury is an ongoing threat of enforcement, not retrospective damages. Any vehicle-specific defects (forfeiture, preclusion) can be addressed on remand, but they do not justify expanding Heck beyond its doctrinal rationale.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Heck v. Humphrey “favorable-termination” bar prevents a § 1983 plaintiff from pursuing prospective declaratory and injunctive relief challenging the constitutionality of a municipal policy when the plaintiff has an outstanding criminal conviction related to the challenged enforcement.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (as limited by the Heck v. Humphrey doctrine) and the First and Fourteenth Amendments (free speech/assembly and due process) as applied to municipal enforcement policies.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Olivier argues that the Fifth Circuit applied Heck too broadly by using his existing conviction to block forward-looking relief (declaratory and injunctive) aimed at preventing future enforcement of an allegedly unconstitutional city policy. He contends that Heck is principally a damages-bar designed to prevent collateral attacks on convictions that must instead proceed via habeas, and that prospective relief—especially relief that regulates future enforcement rather than invalidating the past conviction—should remain available under § 1983. Petitioner and supporting amici frame the issue as important for protecting First Amendment activity from recurring enforcement and for ensuring that unconstitutional local policies can be enjoined even when a plaintiff has been convicted under or alongside the challenged regime.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The City of Brandon argues that Olivier’s suit is an improper end-run around his criminal judgment: the requested prospective relief would necessarily undermine, call into question, or functionally contradict the validity of his still-outstanding conviction, triggering Heck’s favorable-termination requirement. Respondents also emphasize vehicle and preservation problems (forfeiture/presentment) and contend that, even if Heck did not apply, Olivier’s claims would likely fail or be barred on other grounds (e.g., estoppel or res judicata). The respondent-side amicus underscores institutional concerns for local governments, warning that narrowing Heck for injunction/declaration cases would invite collateral federal litigation that destabilizes final criminal judgments and burdens municipal administration.
key_precedents: Siders v. City of Brandon, Mississippi

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that Edwards v. Balisok requires a functional, not label-driven, inquiry and that relief here may practically undermine an outstanding conviction—reinforces the need to apply Heck’s “necessarily implies” test with discipline, not to adopt a categorical bar. Wilkinson v. Dotson cuts against Justice Thomas’s broader approach by confirming that forward-looking relief can proceed where success would not logically require treating the conviction as invalid; the key is the specific declaration or injunction sought and its logical implications. Because the record and pleadings leave ambiguity about whether the requested prospective relief can be cabined to future enforcement without negating the conviction’s validity, minimalism and institutional legitimacy counsel reversing and remanding for a concrete, claim- and remedy-specific Heck analysis rather than affirming on a broad prophylactic rule. If, on remand, the lower court concludes the only effective decree would necessarily imply invalidity, Heck will bar it; but we should not decide that categorically at this level of generality.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest opposing point, advanced by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan, is that Wilkinson v. Dotson requires a claim- and remedy-specific application of Heck and thus favors a remand for “tailoring.” But Edwards v. Balisok makes clear that labels and artful prospective framing do not control; the question is the necessary legal implication of success, and here a declaration/injunction condemning the enforcement policy that supplied an essential predicate for the still-outstanding conviction would, as Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, necessarily imply that the conviction rests on an unconstitutional basis. Dotson is distinguishable because it involved prospective procedural changes that did not negate the validity of an extant judgment; by contrast, this claim—on this record and as pleaded—targets the substantive validity of the enforcement predicate intertwined with the conviction, triggering Preiser/Heck’s channeling rule. Under a textual and historically constrained understanding of § 1983, we should not expand it into a collateral-review mechanism absent favorable termination, and a remand inviting remedial “crafting” risks precisely the habeas end-run Heck forbids.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s claim-by-claim remand has surface appeal, but it understates what Edwards v. Balisok requires us to do: look to functional effect, not to artful narrowing or labels. On this record, the specific declaration/injunction sought—branding unconstitutional the very enforcement policy that supplied the predicate for Olivier’s conviction—would necessarily imply the invalidity of that still-outstanding judgment, triggering Heck’s bar and preventing a § 1983 end-run around habeas as Preiser contemplated. Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s remedial-tailoring proposal fails at the threshold stage because the logical implications of success, not a court’s later ability to rewrite relief, determine whether Heck applies. Wilkinson v. Dotson does not move me here because Dotson concerned forward-looking procedural changes that left existing judgments intact; this case targets the substantive legality intertwined with the conviction itself.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Alito raise the hardest point: that an injunction/declaration against the same enforcement policy risks becoming a functional end-run around habeas by undermining the predicate for Olivier’s still-valid conviction. But as the Chief Justice notes, Wilkinson v. Dotson makes the controlling inquiry claim- and remedy-specific—whether the particular relief would necessarily imply invalidity—not whether the suit relates to the same policy in some practical sense; that framework leaves room for forward-looking relief that regulates future enforcement without adjudicating the conviction’s lawfulness. Justice Barrett is right (via Edwards v. Balisok) that labels don’t control, yet her approach would effectively convert “necessarily implies” into “would predictably be used to attack,” insulating ongoing municipal practices with serious real-world impacts from any equitable check while expanding Heck beyond its rationale. A narrow remand like Roberts proposes—allowing prospective claims to proceed but requiring denial or tailoring of any decree that would functionally declare the conviction invalid—best preserves finality without closing the courthouse doors to people facing continuing unconstitutional enforcement.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that Edwards v. Balisok requires a functional analysis and prevents plaintiffs from evading Heck by relabeling relief as “prospective”—is right, but it cuts toward a remedy-specific inquiry rather than a categorical bar. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Wilkinson v. Dotson directs us to ask whether the particular decree sought would necessarily imply invalidity; that is a concrete, claim-by-claim question, and some forward-looking injunctions can regulate future enforcement without logically requiring a court to treat Olivier’s conviction as unlawful. Justice Barrett’s view that Heck is a threshold bar doesn’t defeat remand, because the threshold inquiry still requires identifying the operative requested relief and its logical implications, and a remand can direct the lower courts to deny (not “rewrite”) any relief that would entail a legal conclusion inconsistent with the conviction’s continued validity. Pragmatically and textually, that approach preserves Heck’s finality/federalism function (as Justice Thomas stresses) while avoiding an overbroad rule that would disable § 1983 from addressing ongoing practices that can be remedied without repudiating a judgment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Alito’s best point—that Edwards v. Balisok requires a functional, not label-driven, application of Heck “no matter the relief sought”—is correct, but it still leaves the controlling question as Wilkinson v. Dotson frames it: whether success on the particular claim and requested decree would necessarily imply the invalidity of the outstanding conviction. Chief Justice Roberts is right that a claim-by-claim, remedy-specific analysis is more faithful to Heck’s text and rationale than a categorical bar on prospective relief whenever it concerns the same enforcement predicate; otherwise we effectively replace “necessarily imply” with “relates to,” expanding the doctrine beyond its stated limits. Justice Barrett’s concern that remedial narrowing cannot cure a threshold Heck problem has force, but it assumes the requested prospective relief necessarily entails a legal conclusion inconsistent with the conviction—an assumption that should be tested concretely on remand by parsing what declarations/injunctions are actually sought and what they logically entail. Justice Thomas’s finality and federalism concerns are serious, yet they are already accounted for by enforcing the necessary-implication gatekeeping rule without extending it to foreclose forward-looking challenges that can be adjudicated without negating the judgment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s point that Wilkinson v. Dotson frames Heck as a claim- and remedy-specific inquiry and that a remand might allow lower courts to separate permissible prospective regulation from impermissible collateral attack. But as Justice Alito and Justice Barrett emphasize, Edwards v. Balisok requires us to look past labels to functional effect, and on this record the requested declaration/injunction would pronounce unconstitutional the enforcement predicate that produced Olivier’s still-outstanding conviction—success would therefore necessarily imply that the judgment is unlawful. The opposing side’s “remedial tailoring” solution (Justices Kagan and Sotomayor) is administratively unstable because it invites pleading around habeas and pushes Heck’s threshold inquiry into merits-stage rewriting of relief, undermining the finality and channeling principles of Heck and Preiser. I would therefore affirm the bar here while leaving open that truly prospective challenges can proceed where success does not logically call an existing conviction into question.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms a claim- and remedy-specific inquiry, and that forward-looking relief is not categorically barred. But Edwards v. Balisok requires us to look past labels to the functional logic of the decree sought, and here (as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes) the requested declaration/injunction would adjudicate unconstitutional the enforcement policy that supplied the legal predicate for Olivier’s still-outstanding conviction—so success would necessarily imply that the conviction rests on an unlawful basis. I remain unpersuaded by Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s suggestion that remedial narrowing can be deferred to later merits proceedings, because Heck operates as a threshold screen keyed to the relief actually requested and its logical implications, not to a court’s later ability to rewrite the case into a different one. Dotson’s allowance for prospective relief fits procedural or forward-looking adjustments that leave the existing judgment intact; this claim, as pleaded, cannot be granted without functionally repudiating the conviction, which keeps it within Heck/Preiser.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Alito correctly insist, under Edwards v. Balisok and Wilkinson v. Dotson, that we must look to the functional effect of the requested relief and not be misled by prospective labels; if success would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, Heck applies. But that very functional inquiry is claim- and remedy-specific, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, and does not justify a categorical rule that any forward-looking challenge to the same policy is barred. Justice Thomas’s finality and federalism concerns are substantial, yet they are best respected by disciplined remedial tailoring—refusing any declaration that Olivier’s conviction was unconstitutional and narrowing or denying relief that would logically negate it—rather than by insulating ongoing municipal practices from equitable review whenever they relate to a past conviction. On this record, reversal and remand for a concrete application of Heck’s “necessarily implies” test to the particular declaratory/injunctive relief sought remains the procedurally fair and practically workable course.

John Roberts.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars § 1983 claims only when success would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction, a rule grounded in finality and channeling direct attacks into habeas rather than § 1983. A request for forward-looking declaratory and injunctive relief aimed at restraining future enforcement of a municipal policy can be adjudicated on narrow grounds without negating the plaintiff’s past conviction, and dicta in Edwards v. Balisok indicates prospective relief “ordinarily” does not trigger Heck’s favorable-termination requirement. To preserve institutional legitimacy and avoid expanding Heck beyond its rationale, I would hold only that Heck does not categorically bar prospective relief and remand for the lower courts to determine—claim by claim—whether the specific relief sought would in fact necessarily imply invalidity of the existing conviction. This narrow approach respects precedent while preventing an overbroad rule that insulates ongoing municipal policies from First and Fourteenth Amendment review under § 1983.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1983’s text does not authorize using federal civil litigation as a vehicle to collaterally undermine an outstanding state conviction, and Heck v. Humphrey properly enforces that boundary by barring claims whose success would necessarily imply the invalidity of the conviction unless it has been favorably terminated. Where, as alleged here, the requested declaratory and injunctive relief would functionally contradict the legal basis for Olivier’s still-valid judgment, it triggers Heck’s rule even if styled as “prospective” relief, consistent with this Court’s habeas/§ 1983 line in Preiser v. Rodriguez. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms that § 1983 remains available only when success will not necessarily imply invalidity; that limitation is not met when the policy challenge would negate the conviction’s validity. Federalism and finality also counsel against federal courts issuing forward-looking decrees that effectively reopen state criminal judgments without the habeas prerequisites Congress and our precedents require.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars § 1983 actions where success would “necessarily imply” the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, and that principle is not confined to damages labels if the requested declaration or injunction would functionally negate the judgment’s legal basis. Here, Olivier’s prospective relief targets the constitutionality of the municipal enforcement policy that led to (and is intertwined with) his still-valid conviction, so granting it would, as a practical matter, cast that conviction into doubt and invite an end-run around habeas. Edwards v. Balisok confirms that Heck’s favorable-termination rule turns on the necessary-implication test rather than the form of relief, and Wilkinson v. Dotson does not help petitioner where the requested relief would undercut the conviction itself rather than merely regulate future procedures without affecting validity. Preserving finality of criminal judgments and avoiding collateral federal supervision of local enforcement counsel adhering to Heck’s bar absent favorable termination.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars a § 1983 action only when success would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding conviction or sentence, and it was crafted primarily to prevent damages suits from operating as de facto habeas. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson, plaintiffs may pursue prospective declaratory and injunctive relief when victory would not necessarily invalidate the conviction—here, an order regulating future municipal enforcement of an allegedly unconstitutional policy can be framed to avoid contradicting the prior judgment. A contrary rule would insulate ongoing unconstitutional municipal policies from equitable review and disproportionately burden vulnerable speakers by denying forward-looking First and Fourteenth Amendment remedies solely because of a past conviction. The proper course is to allow the prospective claims to proceed under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 while cabining relief to avoid any adjudication that would negate the existing conviction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey limits § 1983 only when success in the civil action would "necessarily imply" the invalidity of an outstanding conviction or sentence, a boundary this Court has emphasized in the habeas/§1983 interface. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson, a plaintiff may pursue prospective declaratory or injunctive relief so long as the requested remedy would regulate future enforcement and would not itself invalidate (or require treating as invalid) the existing conviction or its duration. Olivier’s forward-looking challenge to a municipal policy can therefore proceed under § 1983 to the extent the relief is crafted to avoid contradicting the criminal judgment; any overbroad decree that would functionally negate the conviction can be narrowed at the merits/remedies stage rather than barred at the threshold. This approach best fits § 1983’s text and purposes while preserving Heck’s core anti-collateral-attack function tied to habeas.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars § 1983 claims only when success would "necessarily imply" the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, a limitation rooted in channeling direct attacks on criminal judgments into habeas rather than collateral civil litigation. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson, forward-looking declaratory and injunctive relief may proceed under § 1983 so long as it targets future enforcement and would not itself negate the conviction or require its vacatur; a plaintiff’s past conviction does not automatically extinguish the ability to seek prospective relief against an ongoing municipal policy. Reading Heck to categorically foreclose prospective relief whenever a conviction exists sweeps beyond its rationale and risks denying a remedy for continuing or threatened violations of the First and Fourteenth Amendments. The proper inquiry is specific and textual: whether the particular requested relief, if granted, would necessarily invalidate the conviction; if not, § 1983 remains available.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Heck v. Humphrey, a § 1983 action is barred when success would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction unless that conviction has been favorably terminated. This Court has made clear that the favorable-termination requirement is not limited to damages: Edwards v. Balisok and Wilkinson v. Dotson apply the same necessarily-implies test “no matter the relief sought,” including declaratory or injunctive relief, and thus foreclose suits that would functionally undermine a still-valid criminal judgment. On this record, Olivier’s requested forward-looking declaration/injunction appears to attack the constitutional basis for the very enforcement leading to his conviction, creating an impermissible end-run around habeas and finality interests. Respect for precedent, administrability, and the practical need to protect the finality of criminal judgments support affirmance of the Fifth Circuit’s application of Heck here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars a § 1983 action when success would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction unless that conviction has been favorably terminated, and that principle turns on the logical relationship between the requested relief and the conviction’s validity rather than the label (damages vs. equitable relief). Although § 1983’s text contains no favorable-termination requirement, Heck grounded that limitation in longstanding common-law principles against collateral attacks on extant criminal judgments, and Edwards v. Balisok confirms Heck’s reach beyond pure damages to § 1983 claims where success would negate the basis for the judgment. Here, the requested declaratory and injunctive relief—aimed at declaring unconstitutional the municipal policy under which (or in a way that) plaintiff’s conviction was obtained—would functionally call into question that still-valid conviction, triggering Heck’s bar. Any narrowing to categorically exempt prospective relief would require extending dicta into a rule and would be methodologically inconsistent with Heck’s “necessarily implies” test as applied to the specific relief sought.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey limits § 1983 only when success in the civil action would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction, a doctrine aimed at preventing end-runs around habeas for attacking final criminal judgments. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson, § 1983 remains available for prospective declaratory and injunctive relief that regulates future enforcement and does not itself invalidate (or require invalidation of) the prior conviction; forward-looking relief is “more distant from” Heck’s core concerns. Here, a properly framed challenge to an ongoing municipal policy under the First and Fourteenth Amendments can be adjudicated without disturbing Olivier’s conviction, and barring such suits would create serious practical consequences by insulating unconstitutional policies from review and chilling protected activity. Procedural fairness is better served by allowing prospective relief while preserving Heck’s bar where the requested remedy would functionally negate the criminal judgment.
